sources.title: compute.py: every matrix, sum, count and exhaustive check printed in the paper
sources.venue: Script in this repository, written by the paper's author
sources.notes: Run with python3 -I compute.py; output saved in appendices/compute.out. Pure Python integer arithmetic. Checks statements for small graphs; it is not a proof.

claims.text: For every labelled simple graph with 1 to 4 vertices and k = 0 to 4, every entry of A^k equals the number of walks of length k found by explicit enumeration of vertex sequences: 5525 entries compared, 0 failures. This checks the walk-counting theorem for small graphs; it is not a proof.

In the path graph with vertices n_1,...,n_N and edges n_s n_(s+1), every step changes the vertex index by 1, so every walk from n_1 to n_N has at least N-1 steps; hence the upper limit N-1 of the sum test cannot be lowered. For N = 4 the script gives (A^1)_14 = (A^2)_14 = 0 and (A^3)_14 = 1.
claims.derivation: sections/connectivity.tex, Remark on one power (index argument); numbers by script

claims.text: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran do not define the word 'path' (a search of the extracted text of the paper for 'path' and 'walk' finds no definition). In the proof of their Theorem 1 (p. 16) they identify the (i,i) entry of A^2, which they say equals the degree of the ith vertex, with a number of 'different paths of length 2 between' the ith and jth vertices, so they use 'path' in the sense of walk there, and the proof builds 'paths of length (p + 1)' from 'paths ... of length p' together with an edge. Reading by the author after fetching the paper on 2026-11-06.

support.quote: While the (i, i)th entry of A2G is equal to the number of 10 s in the ith row, and hence equal to the degree of the ith vertex.
